h: Sieges, a vanished lake and nineteen days of partying
p: Before it was a palace, Kenilworth was a fortress, and a seriously tough one. It was founded in the 1120s by Geoffrey de Clinton, and in 1266 it held out through a siege that lasted around six months, one of the longest in medieval English history. A big reason it was so hard to crack was the Mere, a huge artificial lake that wrapped around the castle as a water defence. It's long since been drained, but once you know it was there you can see how the castle sat on its own little island of high ground.
Later, John of Gaunt, son of Edward III, built the great hall in the late fourteenth century, and its tall window frames are still one of the most impressive sights in the ruins.

Then came Dudley's big moment. Elizabeth I's visit in 1575 lasted nineteen days, packed with feasts, fireworks, hunting and pageants, one of the most extravagant bits of royal entertaining of the age. Sadly, after the Civil War Parliament ordered the castle to be made unusable, which is why it's a romantic ruin today. Sir Walter Scott later wrote a whole novel named after the place, which helped turn it into a Victorian tourist hotspot.
Plan two to three hours for castle and garden together. Kids love the climbing, and there's enough open grass to run off steam.

Back in town, Abbey Fields is a big green park with the ruins of the old abbey and a lake, perfect for a picnic. Stoneleigh Abbey is a few miles away for another grand house, and Coventry is close for the cathedrals and the Transport Museum.
